# Trump’s AI Chip Crackdown Inflicts Collateral Damage Across Asia

Washington’s new rulebook spells trouble for a multibillion dollar cloud business helping to power the region’s data center boom.

By Mackenzie Hawkins, Saritha Rai, Kari Soo Lindberg, Philip Heijmans, and Gabrielle Ng

November 22, 2026 at 4:00 PM CST

It was 3 a.m. in Jakarta and the chief executive of one of Indonesia’s largest data center operators, who’d spent hours hitting refresh on the website of the US Department of Commerce until its new rules for chip exports showed up, was on the phone with a top lieutenant. He ordered a damage assessment then headed for the airport and a red-eye flight to Singapore. He needed to meet with Nvidia Corp.’s team in the city-state. 

In the lengthy document it had just published, the US said shipments of advanced chips to four countries in Southeast Asia, including Indonesia, will require Washington’s permission. It also announced a soon-to-come global clampdown on data centers that provide Chinese firms with remote access to advanced hardware they’re restricted from buying themselves.

It’s an industry worth tens of billions of dollars in Southeast Asia, and it risks becoming collateral damage in the superpower AI contest as President Donald Trump returns to the offensive. The US measures, citing national security concerns, are also the most consequential policy change to emerge so far from the scandal engulfing Nvidia. Former boss Jensen Huang was ousted after revelations of his affair with an executive from a customer that is headquartered in Singapore and has links to China.

Trump’s team announced the crackdown in a week that saw AI anxieties deepen across the world’s financial markets — and while the president was on a multi-day tour of Asia, holding talks with regional leaders in the Philippines and later with Xi Jinping in China. For companies and economies in Southeast Asia, which has done well until now out of great-power rivalry, it’s a sharp reminder: what geopolitics gives, it can also take away. 

![Donald Trump Visits Shenzhen, China For APEC Meeting](https://assets.bwbx.io/images/users/iqjWHBFdfxIU/iQWqV9hvXIGA/v1/-1x-1.webp)

China's President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump with other Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation nations’ leaders during the APEC Summit in Shenzhen on Nov. 19. Source: Pool/Getty Images

Outside of the US, the region is among the world’s fastest-growing hubs for data centers. Spending in Malaysia alone is nearing $100 billion. At least $49 billion in credit has been pumped into the industry across the Asia-Pacific area, according to Bloomberg-compiled data, and Southeast Asia has gotten a sizeable slice. It offers builders cheap land and labor, plus proximity to factories that churn out key hardware. Perhaps most importantly, though, it provides access to a huge market in China. 

There are two main ways that China has so far been able to get around export curbs on top Nvidia chips, which the US first imposed in 2022. One is to find ways to buy the chips anyway, breaching the restrictions. The other, which Washington had tolerated, is to rent computing power from data centers that have them, in countries like Malaysia.

There are several companies in Southeast Asia — including Megaspeed International, the epicenter of the Nvidia saga — that the US suspects have dabbled in both methods of serving the China market. Megaspeed has denied smuggling the Nvidia hardware it purchased. In Thailand, one of the most important AI companies, OBON Corp., is suspected by Washington of helping smuggle Nvidia chips worth more than $2 billion to China. OBON hasn’t responded to queries on the matter. 

Thailand’s Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow, who was in Manila for the regional summit, told Bloomberg TV that it was during talks with the Chinese delegation there that news of the US crackdown broke. Asked if the move could set back his country’s ambitions to become a data center hub, he replied, “it could. We have to be more careful now.”

![Philippines Hosts ASEAN Summit And Related Meetings](https://assets.bwbx.io/images/users/iqjWHBFdfxIU/iRiid3FmMLKI/v1/-1x-1.webp)

Thailand's Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow at the ASEAN Foreign Ministers' meeting in Manila. Photographer: Jam Sta Rosa/Pool/Getty Images

In Singapore, authorities said the impact on hardware transshipment through the city-state is manageable, and the top concern is access to chips for domestic use.

The Indonesian data-center boss who’d gone there hoping to meet with Nvidia — to get reassurance that contracts would be honored — didn’t have much luck.

Just a few days earlier the chipmaker’s team had been eager to talk. Now everyone of consequence was suddenly out of town, the CEO was told, according to his lieutenant, who asked not to be identified given the sensitivity of the situation. The company is still confused about how the rules will work, the lieutenant said. Nvidia didn't respond to a request for comment. 

The US restrictions are aimed at slowing China’s AI industry, and they triggered a slump for tech companies like Tencent Holdings Ltd., which acknowledged that progress would likely be set back. The stock has plunged more than 10% since the announcement. 

But both aspects of the new rulebook will squeeze the so-called neoclouds in Southeast Asia too. License requirements for chip exports, designed to address illicit diversion, may slow down imports for all buyers. And the clampdown on remote access, due to take effect in February, will undercut their core business model — raising questions about who’ll use all the computing power they’ve amassed.

The research firm SemiAnalysis says its data shows that Chinese firms tap around 300 megawatts of AI computing power via neoclouds across four Asian countries. 

There’s a lot more in the pipeline, under construction in places like Johor in Malaysia — Southeast Asia’s data center capital, just across the strait from Singapore. Last week, cranes worked through heavy rain, tractors rolled across fields of wet clay and yellow-vested builders buzzed around them. 

![Malaysia Data Center](https://assets.bwbx.io/images/users/iqjWHBFdfxIU/idWWsU0TtV4k/v1/-1x-1.webp)

Ongoing construction at the Bridge Data Centre MY07 hyperscale data center campus in Johor, Malaysia, on Nov. 21. Photographer: Samsul Said/Bloomberg

The buildout in Malaysia has outpaced regional peers, and even globally only the US and China have seen more spending, according to a recent HSBC report, citing the company's data and BloombergNEF. That now leaves the country “in a precarious situation,” said Neil Shah, vice president of research at tech analysis firm Counterpoint, especially because Chinese firms like ByteDance and Alibaba have driven a big chunk of the investment.

Banks that lent to Southeast Asian data centers powering Chinese tech giants are taking a closer look at their books and evaluating any potential fallout. This includes JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Citigroup Inc., which financed a data center operator that once counted Megaspeed among its clients. 

It foreshadows risks for other projects. “In the worst-case scenario,” according to Adib Zalkapli — founder of Kuala Lumpur-based geopolitical risk consultancy Viewfinder Global Affairs — “we may see abandoned, incomplete data centers.”

That’s an outcome Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim had been trying to avoid, after a series of warning shots from the US about Southeast Asia’s suspected role in chip smuggling.

In early 2025 the outgoing Biden administration announced rules to cap exports to most of the world, under a tiered system that also restricted Chinese firms from renting the chips they couldn’t buy. Trump decided not to enforce those measures just before they were due to take effect in May of that year, but the groundwork had been laid.

Weeks later, reports emerged that the US planned to restrict shipments of AI chips to Malaysia and Thailand, adding them to a list of some 40 countries beyond China that were already subject to such rules. Singapore, which had mounted a robust diplomatic response to smuggling allegations earlier that year, was spared. Anwar was determined that Malaysia should be, too.

During an Asean summit in Kuala Lumpur, he pressed US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the issue, according to people briefed on their talks. (The Malaysian premier’s office didn’t respond to a request for comment, while a State Department spokesperson referred Bloomberg to a public readout of the meeting). Soon after, in an unprecedented show of cooperation on export controls, Malaysia announced it would impose its own security measures on shipments of American AI chips, and it later agreed to fully match US rules. 

![MALAYSIA-US-ASEAN-DIPLOMACY](https://assets.bwbx.io/images/users/iqjWHBFdfxIU/iNmZOTbc1Mq0/v1/-1x-1.webp)

Marco Rubio, left, met with Anwar Ibrahim at the Prime Minister's Office at Parliament during the Asean summit in Kuala Lumpur in July 2025. Photographer: Mandel Ngan/POOL/AFP/Getty Images

The US administration’s China hawks had failed to push through what many saw as a necessary step to curtail China’s access to American computing power. They failed again earlier this year, when a draft rule to impose global curbs on AI chip exports got withdrawn. 

But then came the Megaspeed scandal and the fall of Huang, who’d used his close relationship with the president to secure looser export rules. The hawks now have the upper hand again.

They still have to enforce their new policy, something the US has struggled to do with chip export controls in the past. Imposing rules on the cloud, as well as physical hardware, could prove even tougher — and there are already signs not everyone intends to comply.

One Chinese data center developer, according to a person familiar with the company’s thinking, is pausing its plans for an AI facility in Johor. Yet it’s going ahead with a project in Spain, where it’s actively working to secure a Western neocloud partner to buy Nvidia GB300 chips, with a major Chinese AI company as the intended user. This is exactly what the US rules are designed to restrict.

It remains to be seen how much damage the new export controls will do to the broader US-China relationship. Trump and Xi didn’t dwell on it last week, though the Ministry of Commerce in Beijing had already warned that “if the US persists, China will take countermeasures.”

In Southeast Asia, most economists don’t reckon the immediate blow will be too severe. Asia’s manufacturers are enjoying an export boom, sending chips and other components across the Pacific to equip data centers in the US, and that trade won’t be significantly affected by Washington’s new rules.

Even in Malaysia, Capital Economics estimates the hit at around 0.2% of GDP in 2027 and 2028, which would still leave the economy expanding at a healthy pace. For Indonesia and Thailand, the impact may be more in the future — cutting off a promising avenue for growth — than the present.

In the longer run, balancing between the world’s two main AI powers will only get harder, according to Reema Bhattacharya at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft in Singapore. The US and China have competing initiatives for AI governance, and Southeast Asian nations are split between them, though more are in the Chinese camp. Countries will face “increasingly difficult choices about which markets and technology ecosystems they can serve,” Bhattacharya said.

As for Southeast Asia’s neoclouds, the immediate challenge is to find customers who’ll replace their current Chinese ones.

![Malaysia Data Center](https://assets.bwbx.io/images/users/iqjWHBFdfxIU/iIgZ512PGXGM/v1/-1x-1.webp)

A Huashi (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd data center site in Johor. Photographer: Samsul Said/Bloomberg

To be sure, some saw Washington’s move coming, albeit not necessarily so soon. Nvidia has been urging customers for months to limit their Chinese clientele to less than half their overall customer base. 

Nicholas Chia, the CEO of Aolani Cloud — which gets much of its business from ByteDance — said around half of its signed total contract value is directed to Western clients with more on the way. Still, executives are planning an urgent US trip to speak with regulators and considering even more drastic steps, such as relocating to the US.

In Silicon Valley, some hawkish tech workers have for months been discussing whether to buy up computing power in the region to prevent it from going to China’s AI players, according to people involved in the talks. Now Washington has taken care of that, these firms need to decide how much of it they actually want.

![Inside the Aolani Cloud at the Exsim Hyperscale Data Center](https://assets.bwbx.io/images/users/iqjWHBFdfxIU/iWED3Hg8zc1M/v1/-1x-1.webp)

An Aolani Cloud data room at the Exsim Hyperscale Data Centre in Kuala Lumpur. Photographer: Samsul Said/Bloomberg

Another worry centers around Nvidia itself. Under many neocloud deals, the biggest user of Nvidia chips is none other than the chipmaker itself. And while Jensen Huang was a vociferous supporter of what some critics have called “circular financing,” the ouster of “Mr. Jacket” — as the ex-CEO has been dubbed by Asian tech bosses in their messaging groups — could throw that system into disarray. 

On an earnings call last Tuesday, new chief Colette Kress said that Nvidia will be taking a “very strong look” at who it helps out, and that customers including neoclouds will have to line up users for the chips they’re buying.

In the short run, said Malaysia’s former Deputy Trade Minister Ong Kian Ming, it’s unlikely that “local or regional demand can ramp up in time to make up for the loss of demand from China-related sources.” So the region’s best bet, he said, may be persuading the divided Trump administration to soften its new stance.

![CHINA-APEC-DIPLOMACY-SUMMIT](https://assets.bwbx.io/images/users/iqjWHBFdfxIU/i_hWV3lEvHN0/v1/-1x-1.webp)

Donald Trump and Xi Jinping react to musicians' performance as they arrive at the Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in Shenzhen, on Nov. 19, 2026. Photographer: Mark Schiefelbein/POOL/AFP/Getty Images

Before his meeting with Xi, Trump said he was against AI curbs that would “ stifle” the industry. The message in Manila a couple of days earlier, at the dinner with Southeast Asian leaders, was perhaps less promising.

The US is far ahead of everyone else in the technology, Trump said, “and we’ll keep it that way.”

— With assistance from Newley Purnell, Claire Jiao, Sheryl Tian Tong Lee, and Yuan Gao
